guide_description: Three days across Munich's three distinct registers: the compact Altstadt with its markets, royal apartments and beer halls; the museum quarter of Maxvorstadt running east into the Englischer Garten; and the Wittelsbach summer palace and 1972 Olympic grounds in the western districts. Beer garden time is built into the schedule as a stop in its own right, which is how Munich actually works.

days.cluster_name: The Altstadt and the Beer Halls
days.cluster_tagline: A medieval market square, the Wittelsbach state rooms, and a liter of beer under vaulted ceilings
days.neighborhood_description: Munich's historic core sits inside the ring of the old city walls and can be crossed on foot in about twenty minutes. Marienplatz anchors it at the center, the Residenz complex spreads north toward Odeonsplatz, and the daily food market and the oldest beer halls sit within a few blocks in either direction. The area empties of residents after work, so mornings feel like a working city and evenings feel like a stage set.

morning.notes: The Glockenspiel in the Neues Rathaus tower typically performs at 11:00 and 12:00 year round with an additional afternoon show in the warmer months; confirm current times with the city tourist office before planning around it. The show is genuinely underwhelming and everyone watches it once anyway. Skip the town hall tower and climb Alter Peter instead, 306 steps with no elevator, for the best view in the city looking back across the square toward the Frauenkirche. Arrive before 10:00 if you want the square without the tour groups.

afternoon.notes: The former royal palace of the Wittelsbachs is far larger inside than the street facade suggests, and 150 minutes is the realistic minimum. The Antiquarium, a barrel-vaulted Renaissance hall running the length of a city block, is the single room worth the visit on its own. The Treasury and the rococo Cuvillies Theatre are ticketed separately from the palace rooms, so decide in advance which combination you want. Eat first at Viktualienmarkt on the way, since the palace has limited food and you will be inside for a while.

evening.notes: The most famous beer hall in the world, enormous, loud, and overwhelmingly visitors, and worth exactly one evening for the spectacle of the brass band and the vaulted Schwemme on the ground floor. Tables are shared here as everywhere in Bavaria; ask Ist hier frei and sit down. A Mass is a full liter and a Halbe is half that, which matters more than people expect. If you want the same food with a local crowd, Augustiner-Keller near the Hauptbahnhof or the Viktualienmarkt beer garden are the honest alternatives ten minutes away.

if_time_permits.notes: The daily food market just south of Marienplatz, open Monday through Saturday and closed Sunday like nearly everything else in Bavaria. Cheese, charcuterie, produce, and a beer garden in the middle that rotates through the six Munich breweries by season. Prices run tourist-adjusted, the quality does not. The best use of it is assembling a picnic and carrying it into a self-service beer garden later, which Bavarian law explicitly protects.

The twin onion domes are the Munich silhouette and a city ordinance still restricts new construction from rising above them. The interior is austere and considerably plainer than the exterior promises, having been rebuilt after heavy war damage. Look for the Teufelstritt, a dark footprint in the floor tile near the west entrance, and the legend attached to it. Tower access has been intermittent during long-running restoration work, so check before counting on the view.

days.cluster_name: Maxvorstadt Museums and the English Garden
days.cluster_tagline: Old masters in the morning, river surfers at midday, and a brass band in a Chinese pagoda by evening
days.neighborhood_description: Maxvorstadt is the university and museum district north of the Altstadt, holding five major art museums within a few blocks of one another. Walk east and the grid opens into the Englischer Garten, larger than Central Park and running four kilometers north along the Isar. The southern end is busy and social, the northern reaches are quiet enough for actual walking.

morning.notes: One of the great old master collections in Europe, built on four centuries of Wittelsbach acquisition. The Rubens holdings are the largest anywhere and the Altdorfer Battle of Alexander at Issus on the upper floor is worth crossing the city for on its own. Two hours covers the highlights honestly; a full day is possible if you are the kind of person who reads wall text. Bavarian state museums have long charged a reduced Sunday admission, which brings crowds accordingly, so a weekday morning is calmer.

walk_to_next.to: Englischer Garten and the Eisbach wave

afternoon.activity_title: Englischer Garten and the Eisbach wave
afternoon.notes: Enter at the southern tip near the Haus der Kunst, where a standing wave on the Eisbach channel draws surfers in wetsuits year round, including in snow. Watching is free and constant and takes about fifteen minutes to stop feeling surreal. From there walk north along the water past the Monopteros hill, which gives the best skyline view in the park. Nude sunbathing is legal and unremarkable in the designated meadows; nobody will comment either way.

evening.notes: Around 7,000 seats under chestnut trees with a brass band playing from the wooden pagoda on reasonable afternoons. The self-service section allows outside food, so a Viktualienmarkt picnic is entirely welcome here; buy the beer on site. There is a deposit on the mug, returned when you bring it back. Beer gardens run roughly April through October depending on weather, and Seehaus at Kleinhesseloher See is the quieter and prettier option twenty minutes further north if this one is full.

if_time_permits.notes: The best Blaue Reiter collection in existence, built largely on a single donation from Gabriele Munter, with Kandinsky, Marc, Macke and Munter herself hung together in the rooms where the movement makes most sense. The building is a converted Florentine-style villa with a modern wing, and the garden courtyard is a good place to sit. Consistently less crowded than the Pinakotheken four blocks away.

Built on the site of the former Nazi party headquarters, this documentation centre covers Munich's role as the birthplace and administrative home of the movement. Sober, dense, and almost entirely text and photographs, which makes an audio guide worthwhile. It provides the context a city otherwise presented as beer and baroque needs. Pair it with Dachau only if you have the emotional room for both in one trip, not the same day.

days.cluster_tagline: A baroque summer palace, the world's largest beer garden, and the 1972 tented roof at sunset
days.neighborhood_description: West and north of the center, Munich turns residential and green. Nymphenburg Palace sits at the end of a formal canal with a park stretching behind it, the Hirschgarten fills a clearing a short walk east, and the Olympiapark occupies a hill built from war rubble further north. Distances here are larger than in the Altstadt and the tram and U-Bahn do the connecting work.

morning.notes: The Wittelsbach summer residence, reached by tram 17 from the Hauptbahnhof in about twenty minutes. Inside, the Gallery of Beauties commissioned by Ludwig I is the memorable oddity, thirty-six portraits of women he considered worth painting, court rank disregarded. The Marstallmuseum in the south wing holds the royal carriages including Ludwig II's gilded night sleigh. The park behind the palace is free and enormous, with the Amalienburg hunting lodge hidden in it and worth the detour.

afternoon.notes: The largest beer garden in the world at roughly 8,000 seats, with a deer enclosure at one end and a crowd that runs heavily local and family. Augustiner on tap, poured from wooden barrels at the counter, which Munich residents will tell you is the right way to drink it. This is the natural lunch stop of the day: Schweinshaxe, Obatzda with a pretzel, or Leberkas in a roll, all cash friendly and much of it cash only. Open seasonally like all beer gardens, roughly spring through early autumn.

evening.notes: The walk from Hirschgarten is long enough that the sensible move is the tram to Rotkreuzplatz and the U1 to Olympiazentrum, about fifteen minutes door to door. Frei Otto's tented acrylic roof still looks like it arrived from a more optimistic future, and the Olympiaberg, a hill made from wartime rubble, gives a free sunset view over the whole structure with the Alps visible to the south on clear days. The Olympiaturm observation deck is ticketed and open late; confirm current hours before making it the plan. A memorial to the eleven Israeli athletes and one German officer killed in 1972 stands near the Connollystrasse edge of the site and is easy to miss.

if_time_permits.notes: The silver bowl building next to the four-cylinder BMW headquarters tower, covering aero engines, motorcycles, and the postwar cars that saved the company. BMW Welt across the footbridge is free and functions as a showroom and delivery centre, impressive architecturally and thin on substance. The museum is the paid one and the better one. Closed Mondays as a rule, so check before crossing the city for it.

Immediately north of the Nymphenburg park and almost always overlooked by visitors heading straight back to the tram. Twenty hectares of outdoor collections plus a set of glasshouses including a genuinely good tropical and orchid house, which makes it a reliable option when Munich weather turns. The rhododendron grove peaks in May and the arboretum is at its best in October.
